summary: This document updates the MPLS Transport Profile linear protection mechanism in APS mode defined in RFC 7271. It adds rules for initializing the Protection State Coordination logic, the state machine that decides which path carries traffic, and for operating in this mode.

plainLanguage.summary: It fixes some start-up rules for a backup system so that two ends of a link agree from the beginning about which path to use.

questions: psc state machine aps mode updates
what does the psc control logic do at startup
what is the ignore flag in mpls-tp aps
how does mpls-tp aps handle a node reboot
subtitle: Fixes how an MPLS-TP protection switch starts up, so both ends agree on which path to use after a reboot.

tldr.problem: RFC 7271 assumes both ends of a linear protection domain start in the Normal state, but never says what a node should do when it initializes, for example after rebooting while its peer keeps running.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8234 lists the actions the Protection State Coordination (PSC) Control Logic MUST take at initialization, changes four cells of the remote state transition table, and clarifies how the table lookup treats the ignore flag and a cleared protection-path failure.
tldr.outcome: The two end nodes converge to the same local and remote states after a restart, with fewer traffic switchovers. It updates RFC 7271 and stays compatible with it.

today: RFC 8234 is a Proposed Standard from August 2017 that updates RFC 7271, and it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Gap in RFC 7271
sections.content:
MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) linear protection in Automatic Protection Switching (APS) mode is defined in RFC 7271. It offers alternate and additional mechanisms for some of the linear protection functions described in RFC 6378.

Neither document describes what happens when the Protection State Coordination (PSC) Control Logic, the place where the state machine lives, is initialized. Many people assume the state machine starts at the Normal state, but this is not written down, and implementers and the MPLS working group mailing list raised questions about it.

The state machine in RFC 7271 assumes both end nodes of a protection domain start in the Normal state. If one node reboots while the other keeps running, various problematic scenarios can arise. RFC 8234 resolves them and aims to minimize traffic disruption for both cold and warm reboots that require re-initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook only said what to do when both players start the game together. It said nothing about what to do when one player leaves and comes back mid-game.

sections.title: Initialization Behavior
sections.content:
When the PSC Control Logic is initialized, a node MUST do the following:

  • Stop the Wait-to-Restore (WTR) timer if it is running.
  • Clear any operator command in the Local Request Logic.
  • If an SF-W or SF-P (signal fail on the working or protection path) is the highest local request, start at the PF:W:L or UA:P:L state, respectively.
  • If there is no local request and the node does not remember the active path, or remembers the working path as active, start at the Normal state.
  • If there is no local request and the node remembers the protection path as active, start at the WTR state sending NR(0,1), or at the DNR (Do-not-Revert) state sending DNR(0,1), depending on whether the configuration allows automatic reversion to Normal.

Remembering the active path minimizes traffic switchovers while the remote node is still running. This is fine even if the remembered path is no longer valid because of a local input at the remote node during the outage.

In some restarts, such as a cold reboot, no valid SF/SD indications may be present yet. The logic then restarts as if there were no local requests, and a valid indication detected later triggers a state change.
sections.plainLanguage: A node that comes back first checks for broken roads. If none, it uses the road it remembers using, so traffic does not get moved around needlessly.

sections.title: Signal Degrade and the First Message
sections.content:
Two further initialization rules deal with the first message from the peer. If a local Signal Degrade (SD) exists, it MUST be treated as an input to the Local Request Logic only after the local node has received the first protocol message from the remote node and finished processing it. Processing means updating the PSC Control Logic and deciding which action, if any, goes to the PSC Message Generator.

If the first protocol message received after initialization is an EXER (Exercise) message and the remote EXER becomes the top-priority global request, the local node MUST set the position of the bridge and selector according to the Path value in the EXER message and move to the E::R state.
sections.plainLanguage: Before reacting to a wobbly road, the restarted node first listens to what its partner says. If the partner is only running a practice drill, the node copies the partner's road choice.

sections.title: State Transition Modification
sections.content:
Four cells of the remote state transition table need to change so that the two end nodes converge after initialization. These are the DNR entries in the rows for states N (Normal), PF:W:R and PF:DW:R; the Normal row also changes in the WTR column, which becomes note (13). The change in the two protecting-failure rows replaces note (10) with DNR, so note (10) is no longer needed.

The three resulting rows are shown in the table below. The letter i means ignore and N means the Normal state.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook has a lookup table saying what to do for each message. Four boxes in the table were changed so both players land on the same answer.

sections.title: Table Lookup and the Ignore Flag
sections.content:
RFC 8234 adds a rule to the lookup rules in Section 11 of RFC 7271. When a local SF-P is cleared and the priorities of local and remote requests are re-evaluated, the last received remote message may no longer be valid because the protection path had failed. That message MUST be treated as if it were NR (No Request), and only the local request is evaluated.

It also rewrites the last paragraph of Section 11 of RFC 7271. The letter i becomes an ignore flag: if set, the top-priority global request is ignored.

  • If re-evaluation is triggered and the flag is set, the state machine moves to the supposed state, which can be Normal or DNR as the footnotes of the table in Section 11.1 of RFC 7271 indicate.
  • If re-evaluation is not triggered and the flag is set, the machine stays in the current state and keeps sending the current PSC message.
  • If the flag is not set, the machine moves to the state given in the table cell.
sections.plainLanguage: When a broken road is fixed, the old message from the partner might be out of date, so the node pretends the partner said nothing and decides for itself.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The document states that it does not introduce backward compatibility issues with implementations of RFC 7271. If a node implementing RFC 8234 restarts, the new state changes cause no problems at a remote node running RFC 7271, and both ends converge to the same local and remote states. If a node implementing RFC 7271 restarts, the two ends behave as they do today.

The authors also state that the changes to the state transition table were examined to make sure no new problems are introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new versions can still play together. The new version just helps them settle quicker after one restarts.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: No specific security issue is raised beyond those already documented in RFC 7271. The text notes that tightening the description of initializing behavior may help protect networks from restart attacks. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Clear start-up rules make it harder for a trouble-maker to confuse a node that is restarting.
